framework_meta_note: CRS is a commercial-aerospace-heavy specialty alloy producer (Tier-3 defense per cohort metadata). The 10-K does not name any specific Pentagon Program Element (PE number), program-of-record, IDIQ, or DoD prime customer. Defense exposure is only stated at the aggregate end-market level (62% A&D in FY2025). The J-Book divergence framework therefore has nothing to verify against — the dominant signal is UNVERIFIABLE-by-disclosure-design, not RED_FLAG_NEGATIVE. USAspending shows only ~$3.3M of direct DoD prime obligations across multiple years for Carpenter + Latrobe Specialty Metals subsidiary — confirming Carpenter is primarily a sub-tier material supplier into prime contractors (commercial OEMs + defense OEMs), not a named DoD program counterparty.

scores.claim_text: Aerospace and Defense end-use market accounted for $1,768.6M (62%) of FY2025 net sales.
supports: pentagon_jbook(contractor='Carpenter Technology') → NOT_FOUND (no PE in the 410-PE corpus names Carpenter as a prime/sub).

usaspending DoD-prime obligations to 'Carpenter Technology Corporation' + 'Latrobe Specialty Metals' total only ~$3.14M across 5 awards (steel buffer / bearing grade material for strategic stockpile, agency_slug 'department-of-defense'). Vastly below the $1,768.6M A&D bucket → confirms revenue flows through commercial-aerospace OEMs and tier-1/2 defense primes, NOT direct DoD prime contracts.
scores.M_value: NOT_FOUND in J-Book; $3.14M / 5 awards direct DoD prime
scores.interpretation: The 62% A&D claim is factually disclosed and quantified, but the J-Book framework cannot grade it because Carpenter never names a specific DoD program. The orthogonal USAspending check shows direct DoD prime exposure is immaterial (~0.1% of revenue), consistent with the cohort metadata 'mostly commercial A&D exposure'. Score UNVERIFIABLE per J-Book heuristic 7 (NOT_FOUND ≠ red flag when no specific PE was named to look up).

scores.claim_text: Specialty alloys for critical applications in aerospace, defense, medical, transportation, energy, industrial and consumer markets.
supports: pentagon_jbook(program='F-35') → 2 matches: F-35 C2D2 PE 0604840F (RDT&E) FUNDED_STEADY, FY24 $1,236.7M → FY25 $1,134.2M → FY26 $1,182.1M; F-35 Squadrons PE 0207142F (procurement) returned but with null status data in the result.
Carpenter is not named as a primary_contractor on the F-35 C2D2 PE; the J-Book lists this at the prime-integrator level (LM Aero / P&W / Northrop) rather than at sub-tier specialty-alloy suppliers.
scores.M_value: NOT_FOUND by contractor; F-35 program FUNDED_STEADY (downstream proxy)
scores.interpretation: The narrative is generic ('aerospace and defense') and names no specific program. The closest downstream-proxy program (F-35) is FUNDED_STEADY in the J-Book, which would map to PASS for a direct prime — but Carpenter is too far downstream for that signal to be a direct verification. Heuristic 7 applies: UNVERIFIABLE because no specific PE was claimed.

scores.interpretation: Dynamet revenue flows through downstream OEMs (titanium fasteners / medical / sub-tier aerospace), not as a named DoD prime. Filing makes no specific program claim to falsify. UNVERIFIABLE.

scores.claim_text: No single customer accounted for >=10% of net sales in FY2023-FY2025.
supports: Absence of counterparty disclosure at LM and RTX is consistent with sub-tier supplier status (no individual prime would name a specialty-alloy mill in 10-K unless it were a material concentration), but does not directly verify or refute the 10% claim.
scores.interpretation: Counterparty disclosure is silent in both directions — consistent with a non-concentrated sub-tier relationship. UNVERIFIABLE (no falsifying evidence either way).

scores.claim_text: Forward-looking statements depend on combined 'commercial aerospace and defense' cyclicality without breaking out defense.
supports: usaspending(recipient='Carpenter Technology Corporation') → 8 total federal awards, $3.26M cumulative (DoD steel buffer / strategic stockpile + small Latrobe Specialty Metals contracts). Direct federal contracting is ~0.1% of FY2025 revenue.

Combined with C1 finding (62% A&D end-market but zero named programs), the disclosure is structurally vague: it bundles cyclical commercial aerospace + cyclical defense as a single ~62% bucket without telling investors what share is DoD-budget-sensitive vs commercial-build-rate-sensitive.
scores.M_check: usaspending.query_recipient_contracts cross-checked against MD&A disclosure granularity
scores.M_value: $3.26M direct federal / 8 awards across all federal agencies
scores.interpretation: This is the Mode-B finding (implied-verification derivation, per the entity-resolution / two-mode DD heuristic): the 10-K presents a 'defense' narrative leaning on a 62% A&D bucket, but USAspending shows essentially no direct DoD prime relationship. The forward narrative is therefore commercial-aerospace-driven (Boeing / Airbus build rates, engine OEM ramps), not Pentagon-budget driven. Investors who price CRS as a defense beneficiary on rising DoD topline would be misreading the exposure. MODERATE_UNDERDELIVERY — the disclosure is not false, but the framing combines two structurally different demand drivers into one bucket, and the J-Book divergence pattern this cohort tests for is NOT applicable here (no programs named to diverge from). This is a structural disclosure-granularity flag, not a program-funding flag.

jbook_fire_summary.note: pentagon_jbook was queried on all 4 J-Book-grounded claims (C1-C4); only the F-35 program-name query returned a non-empty result. All 4 contractor-name queries returned NOT_FOUND, which per heuristic 7 is UNVERIFIABLE (corpus coverage gap for sub-tier alloy suppliers), not a red flag. Carpenter never names a specific PE in the filing, so the J-Book divergence pattern is structurally inapplicable. The findings re-frame as: CRS forward narrative is commercial-aerospace-build-rate-driven, not DoD-program-driven — investors should not price this as a defense-budget beneficiary.
